analysis.one_liner: Extends pandemic mortgage forbearance and foreclosure protections to all homeowners and strengthens bankruptcy safeguards.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the bill: it was referred to two committees on May 8, 2020, received no further action, and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have expanded the CARES Act's pandemic housing protections. Homeowners with any mortgage — not just ones backed by a federal agency — could have paused payments for up to 12 months with no late fees, and lenders could not have started foreclosures for six months. It also would have protected renters from eviction in buildings whose owners got forbearance, made it easier for families in bankruptcy to keep their homes, and set up government-backed loans so mortgage companies and rental owners could survive while pausing payments. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners whose loans are not federally backed — roughly half the market — who currently had no right to forbearance or foreclosure protection; all borrowers, who would gain up to 12 months of payment pause with no late fees or penalties; renters in buildings whose landlords receive forbearance; and families in bankruptcy, who would get a larger homestead exemption, easier Chapter 13 eligibility, and up to 7 years to catch up on missed mortgage payments.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Homeowners, renters, and families in bankruptcy

how_it_helps.text: Extends the CARES Act's right to pause mortgage payments (forbearance) from federally backed loans to every mortgage on a 1- to 4-unit home, with up to 12 months of forbearance and no fees or penalties beyond normal scheduled interest.
Extends the foreclosure moratorium from the original 60 days to six months after enactment and applies it to all mortgages, not just federally backed ones.
Bars a landlord who receives forbearance from evicting a tenant for nonpayment or charging late fees during the forbearance period.

Raises the federal bankruptcy homestead exemption from $15,000 to $100,000, lets people with COVID-19 hardship discharge Chapter 13 plans after one year, and allows up to 7 years to cure mortgage defaults.
Automatically grants 60-day forbearance to any borrower who falls 60 days delinquent during the covered period, so relief reaches people who do not know to ask for it.
Requires detailed loan-level reporting by servicers receiving federal aid — including race, ethnicity, and geography — so Congress and the public can see who is actually getting relief.

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders and the investors who own mortgage-backed securities, who would wait up to a year for payments they are owed and lose some foreclosure rights; mortgage servicers, who must keep advancing escrow and tax payments during forbearance (offset by access to government loans and loan guarantees under the bill); and the federal government, which would back new liquidity for servicers and rental property owners.

drawbacks.text: Forbearance defers payments rather than canceling them: a household that pauses 12 months still owes the full amount later, which can leave a large lump sum at the end of the loan.

The bill includes a servicer 'safe harbor' shielding companies from lawsuits by mortgage investors over forbearance decisions, and it extends the CFPB's 'GSE patch' — a rule letting lenders make loans that exceed standard debt-to-income limits if they can be sold to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac — which consumer advocates view as weakening underwriting guardrails.

Extending forbearance to all non-federally backed loans imposes obligations on private lenders who received no equivalent federal backing for their portfolios, which lenders argued could tighten private credit.

The liquidity provisions direct Treasury and the Federal Reserve to open existing COVID-19 lending programs to mortgage servicers and large rental property owners, effectively extending federal emergency lending toward financial intermediaries.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core provisions — payment pause, foreclosure moratorium, eviction protections, and bankruptcy safeguards — address an emergency in which millions of households lost income overnight, and the cost falls on lenders and investors in the form of delayed rather than forgiven payments. The main design concerns are that relief is deferral, not cancellation, and that the bill pairs consumer protections with liability shields and expanded federal lending for servicers. On balance it was drafted to protect households during a public-health emergency, and the trade-offs are mostly timing and cost-shifting rather than permanent transfers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Financial Services and Judiciary committees the day it was introduced, never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and expired when the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Wm. Lacy Clay introduced the bill on May 8, 2020, with 24 original cosponsors, and 37 House Democrats cosponsored it in total.
The House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services and, in addition, to the Committee on the Judiciary.
The action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, mortgage lenders and mortgage-backed-securities investors avoided the six-month foreclosure moratorium and expanded forbearance obligations it would have imposed, and servicers avoided the bill's added loss-mitigation and data-reporting requirements. Homeowners facing foreclosure on non-federally backed loans and renters gained nothing from it.

industries.industry: Mortgage lenders and holders of non-federally backed mortgages
industries.note: The bill extends forbearance and a six-month foreclosure moratorium to loans with no federal backing, meaning private lenders and their investors would wait up to a year for payments and lose foreclosure remedies during that window. Their interest in blocking the bill ran against households facing default during the pandemic.

Servicers take on new obligations — advancing escrow payments, offering loss mitigation, and reporting loan-level performance data — but the bill also gives them a liability shield against investors and requires Treasury to open CARES Act lending programs to them so they can fund the forbearance they must offer.

The bill deems servicer forbearance to be standard industry practice and shields servicers and securitization parties from investor lawsuits over it, so investors bear delayed payments with reduced recourse.

The Federal Reserve would be directed to make long-term, low-cost loans to residential rental owners to cover documented rent losses, with payments deferred six months — but only if the owner commits not to evict tenants for nonpayment or charge late fees during the loan.
